## G — Omnichannel Integration

### G.1 — BOPIS (Buy Online Pickup In Store)

**G.1.01 — BOPIS Operating Model for order orchestration**
*Summary:* An operating model pattern for bopis (buy online pickup in store) that explains how the role of order orchestration shapes retail performance beyond generic channel or product analysis.
*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates bopis (buy online pickup in store) into governance cadence, accountable owners, escalation paths, and cross-functional rituals; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during seasonal reset to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is treating vendor tooling as a strategy instead of an operating-model change; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* European grocery and hard-discount tiers typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* G.1.02; retail-v1:G; G.1; operating-model

*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates cross-channel customer identity into margin, cost-to-serve, working capital, and customer lifetime value tradeoffs; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during weekly operating review to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is optimizing the visible KPI while moving cost, inventory, labor, or risk elsewhere; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* specialty apparel and beauty leaders typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.

*Summary:* An operating model pattern for allocation strategies that explains how the role of safety stock shapes retail performance beyond generic channel or product analysis.
*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates allocation strategies into governance cadence, accountable owners, escalation paths, and cross-functional rituals; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during seasonal reset to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is treating vendor tooling as a strategy instead of an operating-model change; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* European grocery and hard-discount tiers typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* I.4.02; retail-v1:I; I.4; operating-model
